name: The Ministry of Jesus
summary: Follow Jesus from his birth in Bethlehem through his Galilean ministry, his journey toward Jerusalem, and his death and resurrection there.

stops.locationNote: Egypt is a region, not a single site — Matthew names no specific town, so a plausible point near the eastern Nile Delta, the traditional route for refugees from Judea, is shown here.
Matthew names no specific site for John's preaching; a general point in the Judean wilderness near the Jordan is shown.
Traditionally identified with the area near Al-Maghtas/Qasr al-Yahud, close to the Jordan's mouth at the Dead Sea, though the exact site of Jesus's baptism is not certain.
Traditionally identified with the Mount of Temptation near Jericho, though Matthew names no specific site.
A traditional site above Tabgha on the Sea of Galilee's north shore, identified since the Byzantine era; Matthew names no specific mountain.
Manuscripts vary between Gadarenes, Gerasenes, and Gergesenes; the eastern shore site is often identified with Kursi.
Herod Antipas's fortress east of the Dead Sea, the traditional site of John the Baptist's imprisonment and execution; not named directly in Matthew's text.
Luke 9:10 places the feeding of the five thousand near Bethsaida; Matthew gives no specific site.

stops.locationNote: Christian tradition identifies Mount Tabor as the site of the transfiguration, though Mount Hermon, closer to Caesarea Philippi, has also been proposed; Matthew names only "a high mountain."
Matthew 19:1 places this teaching in Perea, the region east of the Jordan; no specific town is named.
The upper room's location is not given; a traditional site (the Cenacle on Mount Zion) is shown here.
The high priest's house is not located precisely; a traditional site on Mount Zion (near the Church of St. Peter in Gallicantu) is shown here.
The Roman governor's residence (the Praetorium) is disputed between the Antonia Fortress and Herod's Palace; the Antonia Fortress site, near the Temple Mount, is shown here.
Traditionally identified with the site of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre; the Garden Tomb has also been proposed, though with less scholarly support.
